nodes.description: Balantioides trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa and submucosa and form flask-shaped nests. Chronic invasion can present with nonbloody diarrhea, cramping, halitosis, and abdominal pain and can progress to colonic ulceration.

Balantioides coli infections can be asymptomatic and symptomatic, which can be chronic (with intermittent diarrhoea), or acute (a dysenteric form which can be life-threatening).

nodes.description: Invasive trophozoites can erode the colonic wall and form ulcers. Hyaluronidase activity has been reported and may weaken hyaluronic acid-containing epithelial adhesion, although bacterial co-factors and parasite virulence differences also appear to modify tissue destruction.

evidence.reference_title: Current world status of Balantidium coli.
evidence.snippet: Balantidia produce no known toxins, but their ability to produce ulceration of the colon wall is attributed to hyaluronidase, an enzyme that digests hyaluronic acid

nodes.description: Thick-walled Balantioides cysts ingested in fecally contaminated food or water survive outside the host and initiate infection without an intermediate host.

evidence.reference_title: Current world status of Balantidium coli.
evidence.snippet: Balantidium has a simple life cycle, as follows: dormant cyst to trophozoite and trophozoite to cyst. Transmission is direct, from a contaminated water or food supply to humans

evidence.reference_title: [Colonic balantidiasis: report of a fatal case and review of the literature].
evidence.snippet: Patient receives treatment with amebicide and antibacterial without clinical improvement, presenting as a complication multiple perforation in the sigmoid colon, treated with resection and terminal colostomy.

nodes.description: After cyst ingestion and excystation, trophozoites occupy the cecum and colon. Many hosts remain asymptomatic, but a trophozoite population in the large bowel can progress to tissue invasion and symptomatic colitis.

evidence.reference_title: Current world status of Balantidium coli.
evidence.snippet: Balantidium's habitats in humans are the cecum and colon. Humans may remain asymptomatic, as does the pig, or may develop dysentery similar to that caused by Entamoeba histolytica.

nodes.description: Iodoquinol is an alternative luminal antiprotozoal used for human Balantidium infection when a tetracycline or metronidazole regimen is not preferred.

evidence.snippet: Efective treatments include tetracycline, iodoquinol and 5-nitroimidazole compounds (metronidazole, secnidazole).

nodes.description: Metronidazole is a 5-nitroimidazole alternative used to clear intestinal B. coli infection.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical trials with metronidazole in human balantidiasis.
evidence.snippet: Therapeutic activity of metronidazole against Balantidium coli was evaluated by using two drug regimens in 20 human cases of balantidiasis.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical trials with metronidazole in human balantidiasis.
evidence.snippet: In all patients B. coli disappeared after the 4th day of treatment. Frequent posttreatment stool examination remained negative.

nodes.description: Tetracycline is a drug-of-choice antimicrobial option for intestinal Balantidium infection.
